taxonomy.note: Current Kew accepts Clematis pitcheri and recognizes two varieties, var. pitcheri and var. dictyota. The Central Texas/Edwards Plateau comparison here is species-level, with local evidence centered on var. pitcheri.

evidence: Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Travis County Ranunculaceae herbarium index records Clematis pitcheri var. pitcheri.
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed treatment of Clematis pitcheri var. pitcheri.
Uvalde — Harvard University Herbaria specimen A:01657120 records Clematis pitcheri from the Nueces River west of Uvalde, Texas.
target_zone_range.guardrail: No county inferred from statewide range, ecoregion, cultivation, plant sales, or an unreconciled historical taxonomic concept.

morphology.look_here_first: Look for the nodding leathery urn: dull blue-purple to reddish-purple sepals stay connivent for most of their length, then develop narrow expanded, often crisped/recurved tips.
diagnostic_traits: perennial woody-based climber, usually dying back above ground
leaves simple to 1–2-pinnate; leaflets variable and often prominently reticulate
flowers axillary, usually 1–7, nodding and ovoid-to-urn-shaped
four thick leathery sepals pale to dark bluish/reddish purple
sepal margins narrowly expanded distally and often crispate toward the recurved tip
achene beaks relatively short, about 1–3 cm, nearly glabrous to appressed-pubescent rather than strongly plumose

confusers.separator: C. texensis has true rose-red/scarlet urns with thick non-crispate sepals whose margins are not expanded; C. pitcheri is usually blue/reddish purple and has narrow expanded, crispate distal sepal margins.
Older keys compared these closely. Pitcheri has coarser leaf reticulation and shorter, much less plumose achene beaks; the old reticulata complex has since been taxonomically split.
